label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
# Why I'm keeping the busing project

*(This is mostly for Jess. Everyone else can read it too, but Jess — this one's for you. I'm going to try to explain it once, in one place, instead of us arguing about it in fifteen texts over the next three days.)*

There's a meeting Thursday at 3:15 with Dr. Halvorsen and a parent who would like my project to stop existing. That happened on Tuesday, and since then I've gotten about forty texts, most of them variations on "don't do this," which is fair, and one of them from Jess that was basically "it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it," which half the group chat immediately agreed with.

I'm not mad at Jess. She's being practical. She knows how schools work from the inside — better than I ever will. And she might be right. I want to spend a few hundred words explaining the thing she asked me to explain, which is *why*, not *whether she should agree with me.* If after reading this you still think I'm wrong, I want to hear that from you directly and not in a group chat where we all nod politely and nothing actually gets said.

Here's what the project is, since the complaint made it clear a lot of people have a different idea of it.

I teach US History II. Juniors. Two sections. The unit ends with a project: students interview one person — a family member or someone from their neighborhood — about busing and desegregation in Boston between 1974 and '76. They make a ten-minute recording and write a two-page reflection. That's it. That's the whole assignment.

I've taught at Cobb Street High for four years. This is the third version of the project I've run. No parent has ever complained about it before. Not once. That's not an argument in itself — it might just mean nobody noticed — but it does mean this isn't me doing something new and provocative. It's me doing the same thing I've always done with a unit that I've watched work.

The complaint went to Halvorsen and cc'd a school committee member. Two phrases have been rattling around in my head since Tuesday. The project "reopens wounds." The project "pressures kids to judge their grandparents."

I want to be honest about the second one, because I don't think she's wrong about it, and I don't want to be the guy who dismisses a parent's concern with a lecture about academic freedom.

She's right that there is pressure in it. If I've got a kid whose grandmother was on the wrong side of something, or an uncle who did something ugly in 1974, then asking that kid to go interview him and then write two pages about what he found is asking a lot. Sixteen-year-olds don't have a fully developed sense of what they can survive saying out loud. I know that. I don't need to be persuaded of it. If a kid in my room has an uncle who threw rocks at a school bus and I ask him to go ask his uncle about it, that kid is going to feel something I have no right to tell him he's wrong for feeling.

So I'm changing the assignment. Not killing it — changing it. Here's what Thursday's version will look like: every student gets a real alternative. They can interview the librarian or an archivist instead of a family member. They can work from the recordings I've collected from previous years — the ones families have already let me keep, the ones where the family knows exactly where the audio lives and has agreed to it. They can do the documentary-and-secondary-sources version. The reflection prompts will be the same and the rigor will be the same.

The point is that no kid *has* to interview their family. Ever. If I hand in a version of this where the family interview is the only path and the alternatives are consolation prizes, then the parent is right, and I'd be doing the thing to the kids that she thinks I'm doing. So the alternate option has to be a real option. Not a softer version of the same thing. A real one.

That's also the line, and it's the line I actually care about: the kids who are uncomfortable with this are usually the ones who need it most. And that's exactly why I can't force anybody. I'm not going to stand in front of a room and say *you will ask your grandmother about 1974.* Nobody in my classroom gets cornered. But the project also can't quietly become something else because it was easier and less risky for me. If I do that, then the one kid in each section who's been sitting on a story their whole life — the one who's been waiting for someone to ask — that kid doesn't get asked. And then what was the point?

## What actually happens in the room

In 2023 a kid I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She drove a school bus out of Southie in 1974. He told me afterward that she had never told anyone in that family what she did — not her husband, not her sisters, not him. He said it casually, like it was a mildly interesting fact, and then he played forty seconds of it for the class.

Nobody said a word. For about a minute, the loudest room in the building was completely quiet. I've taught for sixteen years and I've never seen that happen.

Last year a girl found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice — once the day she found out and once the next week. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. She didn't sand it down either. She wrote about what it felt like to hear it from him and what it felt like to sit with it and what she thought about what you owe people who were on the receiving end. It was the most honest thing in that entire batch of papers, and it was honest because she got to choose the shape of the assignment.

Those two kids are why I teach this unit the way I teach it. Not because they're the same kid — they're not, and I'm not building a curriculum around two anecdotes. But because both of them were changed by it, and both of them came out of it okay, and both of them would never have touched that subject if I hadn't put it in front of them as a real question with a real opt-out attached.

And here's the thing the group chat keeps skipping past: this is the history of the city they live in. Not "a topic." Not "a controversial issue." The busing crisis was the largest single event in the history of this city in the twentieth century. My textbook gives it one paragraph, maybe a page and a half, and then we move on to the '80s like the whole thing was an administrative dispute. These kids live five minutes from South Station. Some of them have grandparents who were on school buses. Every single person in my room has an actual, personal, physical relationship to this material whether they've thought about it or not.

The paragraph is what the state decided was enough to teach. I'm not sure the state gets to decide that in my classroom.

## The part where I talk about myself

Jess, you weren't being flippant, and I want to be clear that I'm not taking your text as a betrayal or anything like that. You and I met student teaching in 2012 at the same school, and you were already better at this than I was. You left teaching in 2019 and now you do HR at a biotech in Cambridge, and I imagine you have a completely different set of things you can't afford to lose, and I imagine hearing about a teacher going to bat with a school committee member over a homework assignment made your stomach do a thing. I get it. I really do.

You might even be right. I'd be a lot more comfortable if Halvorsen ran a school where tenure actually meant something, but she still sets my schedule. She still decides who gets AP. And I'd like to tell you those two things don't touch each other, but they do, and everybody in that building knows it, including me.

So no, I'm not doing this from a position of strength. I'm doing it slightly scared, which is, I think, just what it feels like to do anything worth doing in a building where one email can change your life. I want to say that clearly because I don't want people to read this and think I'm being brave. I'm not being brave. I'm being stubborn about one specific thing and terrified about everything else.

## What I'm not doing

I'm not picking a fight with the parent. I want to say that in capital letters, for Jess and for the group chat. She raised something real, she was right that there's a version of this assignment that does pressure kids, and I intend to fix that version. She wrote to my principal and cc'd a school committee member and I am not going to do anything — publicly or privately — that makes her regret having said something. I'm also not going to relitigate her complaint in a blog post, which is partly why I've kept this so factual.

And I'm not trying to win. If Thursday goes badly, if Halvorsen tells me to scrap the unit, I'm going to go teach something else and figure out the next four years. I don't think that's what's going to happen, because she has to run this for two sections of juniors and because I have four years of documentation and a plan to offer her, but I'm not going to pretend I know what she'll do.

The only thing I'm actually trying to do is keep the question in front of the kids.

---

Jess — I'll text you Thursday after the meeting. Probably from the parking lot. Probably something like "it was fine," which will be a lie, and you'll know it's a lie, and you'll ask me a question that takes three texts to answer.

Also: I still think about those student-teaching lunches. You were right about the thing I wrote that first week (I still have it, it's embarrassing) and you were right about the thing I wrote the third week. You've been right about the writing for fourteen years. I'd like to hear what you think about this one, even if it's "no, you shouldn't."

Whatever happens, we're still good? I would very much like for us to still be good.

reasons: The piece says 'I've taught for sixteen years', but the request has the teacher student-teaching in 2012, which means about 13-14 years at most.
The teacher says he will scrap the unit if ordered to, contradicting the stated commitment to retain the project.
